A dweller of Paradise asks Allah to let him farm, and his crop grows mountain-high in a wink; a bedouin says he must be from Quraysh or the Ansar.
The companions were happy on Fridays because an old woman served them cooked silq roots after the Friday prayer, before which they took neither meals nor the midday nap.
Abu Huraira says he narrates much because he stayed with the Prophet while others traded or tended their properties, and after spreading his sheet he forgot nothing of that statement.
The Prophet asks the boy on his right to let elders have his leftover drink, but the boy declines; he also serves a bedouin on his right before Abu Bakr.
The Prophet forbids withholding surplus water, for that keeps people from grazing their cattle.
No blood money is due for death in a mine or well or by an animal, and a fifth of treasure found in one's land is due.
A false oath to take property brings Allah's anger, verse 3.77 confirming it over Al-Ash'ath's well; Allah will not look at one withholding surplus water or swearing falsely over goods.
When an Ansari in an irrigation dispute objects that Az-Zubair is the Prophet's cousin, the Prophet gives Zubair his full right, and Zubair links verse 4.65 to it.
A man who watered a thirsty dog was forgiven, as serving any living being earns reward, and a woman entered Hell for locking up a cat until it starved.
Given a drink, the Prophet asks the boy on his right to let the elders drink first, but the boy declines, so he gives it to him.
The Prophet will drive some people away from his Fount on the Day of Resurrection, as stray camels are driven from a trough.
Had Ishmael's mother left Zamzam as it was, it would be a flowing stream; she let the Jurhum settle by her on condition they had no right to the water.
Allah will not speak to or look at a seller lying on oath about offers, one swearing falsely after Asr to take property, or one withholding surplus water.
No pasture may be reserved as Hima except for Allah and His Apostle; the Prophet made An-Naqi' a Hima, and Umar reserved As-Saraf and Ar-Rabadha for Zakat animals.
Horses bring reward to one keeping them for Allah's cause, shelter to one earning by them, and sin to one keeping them for pride; donkeys fall under the atom's-weight verse.
A finder notes a found thing's container and tie and announces it for a year, then returns it to its owner or uses it; lost sheep are taken, camels left.
Gathering a bundle of firewood and selling it is better than asking people, who may give or refuse.
Hamza, drinking wine, cuts up the she-camels Ali would load with Idhkhir to pay for his wedding banquet, and retorts to the Prophet's rebuke, before drinking was prohibited.
The Ansar decline a land grant in Bahrain unless the emigrants get the same, and the Prophet tells them to be patient with the preference they will see after him.
One of the rights of a she-camel is that it be milked at a place of water.
Fruits of pollinated palms and a sold slave's property go to the seller unless stipulated; Muzabana and similar sales are forbidden, except selling 'Araya dates for ready dates by estimate.
The Prophet pays for Jabir's camel later and mortgages armour for food on credit; Allah repays for a borrower meaning to repay, and he would keep gold only for debts.
The Prophet repays a harsh creditor with an older camel, as the best repay handsomely; a merchant who eased his debtors was forgiven, and Jabir is repaid with extra.
The Prophet blesses Jabir's palms so his father's debts are paid with dates to spare; he seeks refuge from debt and takes on dead believers' debts, heirs getting their property.
Delay by a rich debtor is injustice, a creditor has the right to speak, and one finding his own goods with a bankrupt has most right to them.
A man pledged that his slave would be freed at his death; the Prophet sold the slave to Nu'aim bin Abdullah and gave the price to the owner.
An Israelite lends money for a fixed period; the Prophet measures out Jabir's dates to his dead father's creditors without lessening them, and buys Jabir's tired camel.
A man often cheated in bargaining is told to say 'No deception' whenever he buys, and he did so afterwards.
Allah forbids undutifulness to mothers, burying daughters alive, withholding others' rights and begging, and dislikes idle talk, too many questions and wasting wealth.
Everyone is a guardian responsible for his charge: the ruler for his subjects, a husband for his family, a wife for her husband's house, a servant for his master's property.
A man who recited a verse differently is brought to the Prophet, who says both readings are right and warns that nations before them differed and perished.
After a Muslim slaps a Jew who swore by Moses' superiority, the Prophet forbids preferring him over Moses, whom he will see holding the Throne when all fall unconscious.
A Jew who crushed a girl's head between two stones, named by her nod, confesses, and the Prophet orders his head crushed between two stones.
A man often cheated in buying is told to say 'No cheating' when he buys, and he did so.
A man freed a slave though he had no other property, so the Prophet cancelled it and sold the slave to Nu'aim bin Al-Nahham.
Whoever swears falsely to take a Muslim's property meets an angry Allah; Al-Ash'ath says the verse on oaths sold for little gain came over his land dispute with a Jew.
Hearing Ka'b and Ibn Abi Hadrad argue loudly over a debt in the mosque, the Prophet has Ka'b drop half and tells the debtor to repay the rest.
Umar brings Hisham to the Prophet for reciting Surat al-Furqan differently; the Prophet approves both readings, saying the Quran was revealed in seven ways.
The Prophet says he intended to have the Iqama called and then burn the houses of those who do not attend the prayer.
Abd bin Zam'a and Sa'd dispute a slave-girl's son; the Prophet gives the boy to Abd, as the son goes to the bed's owner, but tells Sauda to screen herself.
